title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 14
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A dry-cleaning chain introduced a same-day service and reports that its revenue per branch has risen. It concludes that customers value speed and will pay for it.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Some branches offer the service only on weekdays.
B. Same-day cleaning uses more energy per garment.
C. The chain closed a third of its branches in the same period, and the surviving branches absorbed their customers.
D. Competitors offer next-day service only.
E. Staff received training for the new service.
questions.explanation: Revenue per branch rises mechanically when branches close and their trade transfers, so the measure moved for a reason unrelated to the service.

questions.prompt: A city replaced its diesel buses with electric ones and reports that street-level air quality on the bus routes has improved. It concludes that the electric fleet caused the improvement.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the conclusion?
options: A. Whether general traffic volumes on those routes changed over the same period
B. How much the electric buses cost
C. Whether passengers prefer the new buses
D. How the electricity used to charge them is generated
E. Whether the buses are quieter
questions.explanation: Buses are a fraction of street traffic; if car and lorry volumes fell too, the improvement is not attributable to the fleet. D matters for total emissions but not for street-level readings on those routes.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain installed faster wireless internet and reports that guest satisfaction scores rose. It plans to install the same equipment in its budget properties to raise their scores.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. The equipment is expensive to maintain.
B. Complaints at the budget properties concern cleanliness and noise, and internet speed is rarely mentioned.
C. Budget guests stay fewer nights on average.
D. Some guests use their own mobile data.
E. Satisfaction scores are collected by email.
questions.explanation: The remedy addresses a constraint that does not bind at these properties, so the same intervention should not be expected to produce the same gain.

questions.prompt: A university library reports that students who use its study spaces achieve higher marks than those who do not, and proposes to expand the study spaces in order to raise marks.
questions.question: The proposal assumes which of the following?
options: A. The library can afford the expansion.
B. Marks are the best measure of learning.
C. The library is open at night.
D. Students who do not currently use the spaces would benefit from them as much as current users appear to.
E. Study spaces are currently full at examination time.
questions.explanation: The inference extends an association observed among self-selecting users to those who have not chosen to use the spaces, which requires that the benefit transfer. E would justify expansion on demand grounds without supporting the claim about marks.

questions.prompt: Every solar farm operated by the Kelsing company that grazes sheep beneath its panels also uses fixed rather than tracking mounts. No site with fixed mounts has required maintenance access more than twice a year. Some Kelsing sites have required maintenance access more often.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Grazing sheep reduces maintenance requirements.
B. Tracking mounts are less reliable than fixed mounts.
C. Most Kelsing sites graze sheep.
D. Sites grazing sheep generate more electricity.
E. Some Kelsing sites do not graze sheep.
questions.explanation: Sites needing frequent access do not have fixed mounts, and grazing implies fixed mounts, so those sites do not graze. B and C assert causal or comparative claims the statements do not support.

questions.prompt: A courier company adopted route-planning software and reports that deliveries per driver per day have risen by 15 per cent. It concludes that the software has made its operation more efficient.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. The software was expensive to license.
B. Drivers report that the routes are sensible.
C. The company simultaneously narrowed its service area, so drivers now cover a denser set of addresses.
D. Some deliveries fail on the first attempt.
E. Fuel consumption per vehicle is unchanged.
questions.explanation: A denser delivery area raises deliveries per day whatever the software does; the two changes are confounded and the second is sufficient on its own.

questions.prompt: A dental practice began sending text reminders and reports that missed appointments fell from 12 per cent to 7 per cent. The practice manager concludes that forgetfulness had been the main cause of missed appointments.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. assumes all patients have mobile telephones
B. ignores the cost of the reminder service
C. does not report the sample size
D. overlooks appointments cancelled in advance
E. treats a reduction produced by reminders as showing that the remaining and prior misses shared a single cause
questions.explanation: A reminder can convert some misses without forgetfulness being the main cause of the original rate; five points of a twelve-point rate leaves most of it unexplained.

questions.prompt: A sports equipment manufacturer notes that players who wear its ankle braces suffer fewer ankle injuries than players who do not, and advertises the brace as injury-preventing.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the advertisement?
options: A. The braces are available in several sizes.
B. Braces are worn mainly by players who have previously been injured and who now also avoid the most dangerous play.
C. Some players find the braces uncomfortable.
D. Ankle injuries are common in the sport.
E. The manufacturer also sells knee supports.
questions.explanation: The behavioural change accompanying brace use offers an alternative cause, and the prior-injury selection means the groups differ in ways that cut against the simple reading.

questions.prompt: A bakery found that apprentices trained by its head baker produce bread rated more highly than bread made by apprentices trained by other staff, and proposes that the head baker train all apprentices.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the proposal?
options: A. The head baker works only in the mornings.
B. Bread is rated by customers rather than by judges.
C. Other staff have been at the bakery for less time.
D. The head baker selects the most promising applicants for personal training.
E. The bakery produces several kinds of bread.
questions.explanation: Selection of the most promising trainees explains the outcome difference without any difference in teaching, so extending the arrangement need not raise the average.

questions.prompt: A telephone repair chain argues that repairing a handset is always better for the environment than replacing it, since manufacturing a new handset generates far more emissions than a repair.
questions.question: The argument is most vulnerable to the objection that it
options: A. overlooks that a repaired handset may be kept only briefly before replacement, so the manufacturing emissions are deferred rather than avoided
B. ignores the cost of repairs to consumers
C. assumes all handsets are repairable
D. does not distinguish between brands
E. relies on figures supplied by manufacturers
questions.explanation: The comparison holds per device only if the repair meaningfully extends service life; otherwise the same manufacture happens later and the repair is added to it.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a proposal to require calorie labelling on restaurant menus argue that it will help customers make informed choices. Opponents reply that studies find only small changes in what customers order.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the opponents' reply as an objection to the proposal?
options: A. Some customers already estimate calories accurately.
B. Labelling is expensive for small restaurants.
C. Restaurants responded to labelling by reformulating dishes, reducing the average calorie content of what is offered.
D. Customers report finding the labels useful.
E. The studies were conducted over short periods.
questions.explanation: Supply-side reformulation delivers the effect without any change in what customers choose, so a small ordering change is compatible with the policy working.

questions.passageTitle: Paying for Work Nobody Can Price
questions.passageText:
A buyer commissioning something that has never been built faces a problem no amount of negotiation removes. A fixed price requires knowing what the work will cost, which is precisely what nobody knows; a contract reimbursing whatever is spent removes the supplier's reason to spend carefully.

The two extremes have symmetrical failures. Under a fixed price, the supplier bears all the risk of cost overrun and therefore prices that risk into the bid, so the buyer pays a premium for uncertainty the supplier cannot control — and when the estimate proves badly wrong, the supplier's remaining options are to cut quality, to litigate, or to fail. Under full reimbursement, the buyer bears the risk and the supplier has no incentive to economise, which is why such contracts are accompanied by armies of auditors whose cost partly offsets what the arrangement was meant to save.

Intermediate forms share the overrun in agreed proportions. These work reasonably where cost can be measured and attributed, and poorly where the buyer keeps changing the specification, since every change gives the supplier a defensible reason for a cost that the sharing formula was not designed to cover.

The consistent finding across public procurement is that the choice of contract matters less than the quality of the specification and the buyer's competence to monitor it. A buyer who cannot say what is wanted, or cannot tell whether it has been delivered, will be poorly served under any contract, and much of the criticism directed at contract type is more accurately directed at that.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, a fixed-price contract for novel work is problematic partly because
options: A. suppliers are prohibited from bidding above cost
B. auditors must verify every expense
C. the buyer cannot change the specification
D. the supplier prices in risk it cannot control, so the buyer pays a premium for uncertainty
E. such contracts are illegal in public procurement
questions.explanation: The passage sets out the symmetrical failures, and this is the fixed-price side. C describes the reimbursement side instead.

questions.passageTitle: Microbes and the Trouble with Association
questions.passageText:
The community of microorganisms in the human gut differs between people who are healthy and people with a wide range of conditions, from metabolic disease to disorders of mood. These differences are real and reproducible. What they mean is a separate question, and the gap between the two has been filled with more confidence than the evidence supports.

Three interpretations fit almost every reported association. The microbial difference may cause the condition; the condition, or its treatment, may alter the microbial community; or a third factor — diet above all — may produce both. Diet is a particularly awkward confounder because it changes gut communities within days and is itself associated with almost every outcome studied.

Attempts to establish direction have relied heavily on transferring microbial communities into germ-free mice. Such experiments have produced striking results, and they carry a limitation that is easy to overlook: a germ-free mouse is a highly abnormal animal, its immune system underdeveloped, and a community transferred from a human into it does not establish itself as it would in a human. The demonstration is that the community can influence a trait in that system, not that it does so in people.

The therapeutic record is instructive. Transplantation of faecal material is decisively effective against one condition — recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection, where the mechanism is displacement of a single pathogen — and results for the broader conditions with which the microbiome has been associated have been modest and inconsistent. That contrast is what a field with one solid mechanism and many correlations should expect.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, diet is an awkward confounder because it
options: A. changes gut communities within days and is associated with almost every outcome studied
B. cannot be measured in survey research
C. varies little between healthy and unhealthy people
D. affects only metabolic conditions
E. is altered by antibiotic treatment
questions.explanation: Both properties are named, which is what makes diet capable of producing the association on both sides.

questions.passageText:
Productivity is output per hour worked. In manufacturing, output can be counted, and the measure means what it says. In much of the service economy it cannot, and the resulting figures are weaker than their use in policy debate suggests.

The difficulty is not laziness. What is the output of a teacher, a nurse, a solicitor? Statistical agencies have often resorted to measuring inputs — hours, staff numbers, spending — which guarantees that measured productivity in those sectors cannot rise, since output is defined as what was put in. Where output measures exist, they frequently count activity rather than result: operations performed rather than health restored, cases closed rather than disputes justly resolved.

The consequences are not merely academic. A hospital that discharges patients faster records higher productivity even if readmissions rise; a school that raises test scores records an improvement whether or not anything durable was learned. Because these measures drive funding and inspection, they change behaviour in the direction of whatever is counted, which is the general problem with any indicator used as a target.

Improvement is possible but partial. Quality adjustment — weighting an operation by the health gain it produces — has been attempted and requires judgements that are themselves contested. The honest position is that service productivity figures are indicative rather than exact, that international comparisons of them are weaker still, and that arguments resting on small differences between such figures are resting on very little.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that measuring service output by inputs guarantees that
options: A. productivity will appear to fall over time
B. quality will be overstated
C. international comparisons will be accurate
D. measured productivity in those sectors cannot rise
E. funding will be allocated efficiently
questions.explanation: If output is defined as what was put in, the ratio cannot improve — which is the specific consequence the passage names.

questions.passageText:
A building conserved for centuries has had its roof replaced, its windows renewed, its stonework cut back and refaced. At some point the question arises of what exactly has been preserved, and different traditions have answered it differently in ways that are worth taking seriously rather than ranking.

The dominant European convention, formalised in a series of twentieth-century charters, privileges original fabric. Repairs should be reversible and distinguishable, replacement minimised, and a ruin stabilised as a ruin rather than completed by conjecture. The reasoning is evidential: the building is a document, and a conjectural restoration destroys evidence while producing something that looks like knowledge.

Other traditions locate authenticity elsewhere. Where timber buildings are periodically rebuilt to the same design by craftspeople trained in an unbroken line, what is transmitted is the form and the technique, and the physical continuity of any particular beam is not what the tradition regards as significant. Treating such a building as inauthentic because its material is recent applies a criterion the tradition never adopted, and the international heritage framework has since been amended to acknowledge this.

The difficulty is that the two criteria genuinely conflict in individual cases. A decayed carving can be conserved as a decayed carving or recut by someone who knows how, and only one of those is possible. What can be asked of any decision is that it state which kind of authenticity it is preserving, and at whose expense — because the pretence that no choice is being made is the one position that is certainly untenable.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that the dominant European convention privileges original fabric on the ground that
options: A. the building is a document, and conjectural restoration destroys evidence while looking like knowledge
B. older materials are more durable
C. replacement is more expensive than repair
D. craft techniques have been lost
E. ruins attract more visitors than restorations
questions.explanation: The reasoning is described as evidential, and the passage adds that repairs should be reversible and distinguishable.

readingPassages.title: What Is Being Preserved?
readingPassages.text:
A building conserved for centuries has had its roof replaced, its windows renewed, its stonework cut back and refaced. At some point the question arises of what exactly has been preserved, and different traditions have answered it differently in ways that are worth taking seriously rather than ranking.

The dominant European convention, formalised in a series of twentieth-century charters, privileges original fabric. Repairs should be reversible and distinguishable, replacement minimised, and a ruin stabilised as a ruin rather than completed by conjecture. The reasoning is evidential: the building is a document, and a conjectural restoration destroys evidence while producing something that looks like knowledge.

Other traditions locate authenticity elsewhere. Where timber buildings are periodically rebuilt to the same design by craftspeople trained in an unbroken line, what is transmitted is the form and the technique, and the physical continuity of any particular beam is not what the tradition regards as significant. Treating such a building as inauthentic because its material is recent applies a criterion the tradition never adopted, and the international heritage framework has since been amended to acknowledge this.

The difficulty is that the two criteria genuinely conflict in individual cases. A decayed carving can be conserved as a decayed carving or recut by someone who knows how, and only one of those is possible. What can be asked of any decision is that it state which kind of authenticity it is preserving, and at whose expense — because the pretence that no choice is being made is the one position that is certainly untenable.
